newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST-S.Africa prime may fall 2 pct point in 97.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-S.Africa prime may fall 2 pct point in 97.

text.p: A two percentage point cut in South Africa's prime rate is possible in 1997 because the country's export performance is expected to improve, the University of Stellenbosch's Bureau for Economic Research (BER) said on Friday.
In its last economic review for 1996, the BER said the recent sharp depreciation of the rand should increase the competitiveness of South African exports.
The overseas economic upswing was likely to strengthen further and this was seen as an additional boost to exports over the next six to 12 months.
"Imports, on the other hand, are likely to be constrained by weaker domestic demand and the rising costs of imports related to the depreciation of the rand," BER said.
All this should result in a meaningful reduction in the current account deficit, which in turn should make for easier money market conditions, it said.
As a result, the pressure on interest rates would be downward and the BER believed a two percentage point reduction in the prime rate next year was a distinct possibility.
"This view could of course be negated should government decide to follow a 'big bang' approach to the removal of exchange control.
"Under such a scenario, the prime rate could increase sharply, by perhaps three to five percent in the short term."
But the BER said the government was unlikely to act in this way in view of its often publicly stated desire to adopt a gradual abolition approach.
The BER said it was concerned that net capital inflows from abroad had been too small to finance the current account deficit.

"In view of the precariously low level of South African gold and foreign reserves, the failure of imports to moderate significantly further, and/or exports to accelerate, in the next six months or so, will invariably necessitate a continued restrictive monetary policy stance in the short term."
